present.explain: An Italian verb's ending says who does it: bevo (I drink), bevi (you drink), beve (he or she drinks); vengo, vieni, viene; voglio, vuoi, vuole, vogliamo. Many common verbs change more than their ending, so learn each one's forms as you meet them.
present.why: Italian changes more verb forms for the person than English does: [[bevo]] already says I drink without io.

examples.means: I drink tea.
examples.literal: I drink tea.

examples.means: You drink coffee.
examples.literal: You drink coffee.

examples.means: He drinks tea.
examples.literal: He drinks tea.

examples.means: He's coming and I'm coming.
examples.literal: He comes and I come.

contrasts.says: Because the ending says who, io and tu can be left out: Bevo caffè.
English drink becomes drinks with he, she or it. Italian distinguishes more people through its verb forms.

mistakes.why: With io, it's bevo.
With tu, it's bevi.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

no-subject.explain: Since the verb's ending says who, Italian usually leaves out io, tu, lui and the rest: Bevo caffè (I drink coffee), Sei pronto? (are you ready?), Mangiamo qui (we're eating here). Say the subject when it matters who, or to contrast two people: Tu sei pronto e io no.
no-subject.why: English needs I or you in front; Italian's ending already says it: [[Bevo]] is I drink, [[Sei]] is you are.

examples.means: I drink coffee with milk.
examples.literal: Drink coffee with milk.

examples.means: Are you ready?
examples.literal: Are ready?

examples.means: We're eating here.
examples.literal: Eat here.

examples.text: Tu sei pronto e io no.
examples.means: You're ready and I'm not.
examples.literal: You are ready and I not.

contrasts.says: The ending does the work: bevo, bevi, beve.
English says I in I drink coffee; Italian can leave io out because bevo already identifies the speaker.

mistakes.why: With io the ending is -o; and io can be left out.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

gender.explain: Italian nouns have a grammatical gender: masculine, as in il telefono and il tavolo, or feminine, as in la borsa and la chiave. The masculine singular article can be il or lo, depending on the following sound. Before a vowel, lo and la become l': l'acqua. Articles and adjectives agree with the noun: un caffè, molto caffè but molta acqua, il mio telefono but la mia chiave. Many feminine nouns end in -a and masculine nouns in -o, but not all (la chiave, il latte), so learn the article with each noun.
gender.why: The noun decides, and the words around it follow: [[il]] telefono, [[la]] borsa.

examples.means: The phone is on the table.
examples.literal: The phone is on the table.

examples.means: The bag is on the table.
examples.literal: The bag is on the table.

examples.means: I drink a lot of water.
examples.literal: Drink much water.

contrasts.says: English has one the; Italian changes its article for gender, number and the following sound.
mio and mia follow the noun the same way: il mio telefono, la mia chiave.

mistakes.why: telefono is an il word.
borsa is a la word.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

question.explain: A yes-or-no question can keep a statement's order, with intonation marking the question: Sei pronto?, La macchina è qui? A question word or phrase normally comes first: Dov'è la macchina? (dove and è run together), Cosa vuoi fare? Italian does not add a helper like English do.
question.why: English often changes the order or adds do; Italian can ask through intonation: [[Sei pronto]]? is you are ready?

examples.means: Are you ready?
examples.literal: Are ready?

examples.means: Is the car here?
examples.literal: The car is here?

examples.means: Where's the car?
examples.literal: Where is the car?

examples.means: What do you want to do?
examples.literal: What want do?

contrasts.says: English often puts is or a helper like do first. Italian can keep the statement order and use intonation.

mistakes.why: One car: è, run together with dove.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

possessive.explain: Italian normally puts an article before mio and tuo: il mio telefono, la mia chiave, il tuo libro, la tua borsa. mio goes with a masculine singular noun and mia with a feminine singular noun. With unmodified singular family words such as madre and padre, standard Italian normally leaves the article out with mio and tuo: mia madre, tuo padre. Regional or expressive uses of an article with family words also exist.
possessive.why: Italian says the my phone: [[il mio]] telefono, [[la mia]] chiave. The form of my agrees with the possessed noun, not the owner.

examples.means: Where's my key?
examples.literal: Where is the my key?

examples.text: Il mio telefono è nella borsa.
examples.means: My phone is in the bag.
examples.literal: The my phone is in the bag.

examples.means: My mother has the key.
examples.literal: My mother has the key.

examples.means: Is that your father?
examples.literal: Is your father?

contrasts.says: il mio with il words, la mia with la words.
English says my phone; Italian says the my phone.

mistakes.why: telefono is masculine: mio, not mia.
madre is feminine: mia, not mio.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

articulated.explain: su (on), in (in) and di (of) run into the after them: su + il is sul, in + la is nella, di + la is della. So: sul tavolo (on the table), nella borsa (in the bag), la chiave della macchina (the key of the car). They're never written apart.
articulated.why: Italian joins the little words: [[sul]] tavolo is su il tavolo, on the table, said and written as one word.

examples.means: The phone is on the table.
examples.literal: The phone is on the table.

examples.means: The key is in the bag.
examples.literal: The key is in the bag.

examples.text: La chiave della macchina è qui.
examples.means: The car key is here.
examples.literal: The key of the car is here.

contrasts.says: sul goes with il words; nella and della with la words.
English writes on the as two words; Italian makes them one.

mistakes.wrong: Il telefono è su il tavolo.
mistakes.why: su and il always run together: sul.

mistakes.wrong: La chiave è in la borsa.
mistakes.why: in and la: nella.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons, open to correction.

negation.explain: non goes before the finite verb and any short object pronouns before it: Non bevo caffè, Lei non viene, Non posso leggere. In these modal constructions, it comes before the modal. English often adds do or does; Italian does not need that helper.
negation.why: To negate the whole statement, put [[non]] before the verb: [[Non]] bevo caffè, not I drink coffee.

examples.means: I don't drink coffee.
examples.literal: Not I drink coffee.

examples.means: He isn't coming home.
examples.literal: He not comes home.

examples.means: I can't read the book.
examples.literal: Not I can read the book.

contrasts.says: English says don't or isn't; Italian says non before the verb.

mistakes.why: With io, use bevo. non stays before the verb.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

modal.explain: After volere (want), potere (can) and dovere (have to), the next verb stays in the infinitive: Voglio mangiare, Puoi leggere questo?, Devo lavorare. The modal changes for the person. No preposition links it to the infinitive, though words such as ancora can come between: Devo ancora lavorare.
modal.why: [[Voglio]] already says I want, so the next verb stays plain: [[Voglio mangiare]], I want eat.

examples.means: I want to drink a coffee.
examples.literal: I want drink a coffee.

examples.means: Can you read this?
examples.literal: You can read this?

examples.means: I still have to work.
examples.literal: I must still work.

contrasts.says: The first verb takes the form for who (voglio, vuoi, vuole); the second never does.
English want to has to, whereas can has no to. Italian volere, potere and dovere all take an infinitive without a linking preposition.

mistakes.why: After voglio, the basic form.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

demonstrative.explain: questo goes with an il word and questa with a la word, for this: questo libro, questa chiave. On its own it points at a thing: Questo è un libro, Questa è la mia casa. For that, further away, Italian says quello, which comes later.
demonstrative.why: questo matches the noun like il and la: [[questo]] libro, [[questa]] chiave.

examples.means: I'm reading this book.
examples.literal: I read this book.

examples.means: This key is for you.
examples.literal: This key is for you.

examples.means: This is a book.
examples.literal: This is a book.

contrasts.says: questo with il words, questa with la words.

mistakes.why: libro is an il word: questo.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons, open to correction.

lei-formal.explain: Lei, written with a capital L in these lessons, is the polite you, used when the relationship or situation calls for formality. It takes a third-person singular verb: Lei vuole un caffè?, Lei sa dov'è?, Lei va a casa? tu is the familiar singular you; voi is plural you.
lei-formal.why: [[Lei]] means you in these examples, not she. It takes the same verb form as lui and lei: [[Lei vuole]], you want.

examples.means: Do you want a coffee?
examples.literal: You want a coffee?

examples.text: Lei sa dov'è la mia macchina?
examples.means: Do you know where my car is?
examples.literal: You know where is the my car?

examples.means: This book is for you.
examples.literal: This book is for you.

contrasts.says: Lei takes the lui and lei form: Lei vuole, Lei sa, Lei va.
English has one you; Italian says tu or Lei by who you're talking to.

mistakes.why: With Lei, the lui and lei form.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

c-e.explain: c'è introduces one person, one thing or something you do not count: C'è qualcuno alla porta. ci sono introduces more than one: Ci sono mio padre e mia madre. When people are expected, ci sono can say they are here or present.
c-e.why: English says there is or there are. Italian puts [[ci]] with essere: [[c'è]] for one, [[ci sono]] for more than one.

examples.means: There's someone at the door.
examples.literal: There is someone at the door.

examples.means: There's an open door.
examples.literal: There is a door open.

examples.text: Ci sono mio padre e mia madre.
examples.means: My father and mother are here.
examples.literal: There are my father and my mother.

contrasts.says: The there in there is introduces something; it does not necessarily mean over there.
è goes with one; sono goes with more than one in ci sono.

mistakes.wrong: Ci sono mio padre e mio madre.
mistakes.right: Ci sono mio padre e mia madre.
mistakes.why: mia agrees with madre, a feminine word.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

adjective-after.explain: A describing word often comes after its noun: una porta aperta, an open door. It agrees with the noun: aperto with libro, aperta with porta. Some adjectives can also come before the noun, sometimes with a different emphasis or meaning; position alone does not make a sentence wrong.
adjective-after.why: English normally puts open before door. Italian can put [[aperta]] after [[porta]] while keeping the same meaning.

examples.means: There's an open door.
examples.literal: There is a door open.

examples.means: Is there anyone at the open door?
examples.literal: There is anyone at the door open?

contrasts.says: The ending follows the noun: porta aperta, libro aperto.
English says an open door; Italian says una porta aperta.

mistakes.why: porta is feminine: aperta.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

progressive.explain: stare plus a gerund describes an action in progress. sto cercando means I am looking. The gerund cercando stays the same; sto says who is doing it. The simple present cerco can also describe looking now when the context is clear.
progressive.why: English often uses I am looking for an action happening now. Italian can make that ongoing action explicit with [[sto cercando]].

examples.text: Oggi sto cercando la mia chiave.
examples.means: Today I'm looking for my key.
examples.literal: Today I am looking for the my key.

examples.means: I'm looking in the bag.
examples.literal: I am looking in the bag.

contrasts.says: Cerco la chiave can also mean I am looking for the key.
Sto cercando is happening now; Ho perso describes a loss that has happened.

mistakes.why: With io the form of stare is sto, not sta.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

perfect.explain: Ho perso uses avere plus the past participle perso to report a completed loss. ho says I; hai says you. Here perso stays the same for a male or female speaker. Depending on context, ho perso can mean I lost or I have lost.
perfect.why: The past event uses two pieces: [[ho]] and [[perso]]. Learning perdere with perso helps you recognize this irregular past form.

examples.means: I've lost your key.
examples.literal: I have lost the your key.

examples.text: Hai perso la chiave anche tu?
examples.means: Have you lost the key too?
examples.literal: You have lost the key also you?

contrasts.says: Cerco la chiave describes the search; Ho perso la chiave describes the earlier loss.
Italian uses this form both where English says I lost and where it says I have lost.

mistakes.why: The helper must agree with io: ho.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

verb-preposition.explain: Learn a verb together with its link to the next word. cercare takes the person or thing directly: Cerco la chiave. English needs for in look for; Italian does not add per. A place can still follow with its own preposition: Cerco la chiave in macchina.
verb-preposition.why: The English phrase look for corresponds to one Italian verb, [[cercare]]. The key is its direct object.

examples.means: I'm looking for the key in the car.
examples.literal: I look for the key in car.

examples.means: I have to look for the phone.
examples.literal: I must look for the phone.

contrasts.says: After devo, use cercare in its basic form.
Do not copy the for from look for into Italian; the verb already connects to the thing sought.

mistakes.why: After devo, use the infinitive cercare. The object follows without a preposition.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

time-telling.explain: alle due means at two o'clock. Use it to say when an appointment or another event happens. alle is a and le written together. There is no separate word for o'clock in these sentences.
time-telling.why: English says at two. Italian says [[alle due]], literally at the two, with the article inside alle.

examples.means: I have an appointment at two o'clock.
examples.literal: I have an appointment at the two.

examples.text: Il mio appuntamento è alle due.
examples.means: My appointment is at two o'clock.
examples.literal: The my appointment is at the two.

contrasts.says: a and le join as alle, just as a and la join as alla.
Do not add a word for o'clock after due here.

mistakes.wrong: Ho un appuntamento a le due.
mistakes.why: a and le must be joined as alle in this time expression.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

conditional.explain: vorrei means I would like. It is the conditional of volere for io, and it makes a wish or request softer than voglio, I want. You can put the requested thing straight after it: Vorrei un appuntamento.
conditional.why: Italian puts the would like meaning into one verb, [[vorrei]]. It is different from voglio, rather than a more polite translation of the same form.

examples.text: Vorrei un appuntamento con il medico.
examples.means: I'd like an appointment with the doctor.
examples.literal: I would like an appointment with the doctor.

examples.means: I'd like an appointment today.
examples.literal: I would like an appointment today.

contrasts.says: volere is already familiar in voglio; vorrei is a different form of that verb.
I would like and I want express the same desired thing with different force.

mistakes.why: appuntamento is masculine: un, with no apostrophe before its vowel.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

plural.explain: More than one appuntamento becomes appuntamenti: due appuntamenti. Many masculine nouns ending in -o have a plural in -i, but learn the plural with each noun. Some words, such as caffè, keep the same written form.
plural.why: The number two requires more than one: [[due appuntamenti]]. English adds -s here; Italian changes the ending.

examples.means: I have two appointments today.
examples.literal: I have two appointments today.

examples.means: I'd like two coffees.
examples.literal: I would like two coffees.

contrasts.says: Gender and number both matter when words agree.
appuntamento changes to appuntamenti; caffè stays caffè even after due.

mistakes.why: With due, use the plural appuntamenti.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

infinitive-links.explain: per followed by an infinitive can explain a purpose: soldi per pagare, money to pay. Here per links the money to what it will be used for. Other expressions have other links; do not put per or another preposition before every infinitive.
infinitive-links.why: English uses to in money to pay. Italian uses [[per pagare]] for this purpose, with pagare in its basic form.

examples.text: Lui non ha soldi per pagare.
examples.means: He doesn't have any money to pay.
examples.literal: He not has money for pay.

examples.means: I have money to pay.
examples.literal: I have money for pay.

contrasts.says: In Posso pagare, potere takes the infinitive without per.
English to can correspond to different Italian links, or to no word at all.

mistakes.why: After per expressing this purpose, use the infinitive pagare, not pago.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

piacere.explain: ci piace says that something is pleasing to us: we like it. The thing or activity being liked determines the verb. A single thing, or an infinitive describing an activity, takes piace: Ci piace questo caffè; Ci piace mangiare insieme.
piacere.why: Italian starts from what is pleasing. [[Ci]] means to us here, and [[piace]] matches the coffee or the activity, not us.

examples.means: We like this coffee.
examples.literal: To us is pleasing this coffee.

examples.text: Ci piace mangiare insieme a casa.
examples.means: We like eating together at home.
examples.literal: To us is pleasing eating together at home.

contrasts.says: The English subject is we; in Italian the liked thing or activity is the subject.
ci in ci piace means to us. It has a different job in ci sono, there are.

mistakes.why: One coffee takes piace, even when several people like it.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

avere.explain: avere bisogno di means to need. Keep bisogno unchanged while avere changes with the person: Ho bisogno di aiuto, Hai bisogno di aiuto?, Abbiamo bisogno di aiuto. di connects bisogno to the thing needed.
avere.why: Italian says have need of where English uses need as a verb: [[ho bisogno di]] aiuto.

examples.means: Do you need help?
examples.literal: You have need of help?

examples.means: We need a phone.
examples.literal: We have need of a phone.

examples.text: Mio padre ha bisogno di aiuto.
examples.means: My father needs help.
examples.literal: My father has need of help.

contrasts.says: The form of avere says who needs something: ho, hai, ha, abbiamo.
English need corresponds to the whole expression avere bisogno di.

mistakes.why: With io, use ho. bisogno does not change.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

imperative.explain: chiama is a command to one person you say tu to: Chiama il medico, per favore. For chiamare, the tu command ends in -a. A command asks the listener to act; it normally leaves out tu. per favore adds please.
imperative.why: [[Chiama]] asks someone to call. It has the same written form as the statement form for lui or lei, so the situation tells you which job it is doing.

examples.means: Call the doctor, please.
examples.literal: Call the doctor, please.

examples.means: Give your father a quick call.
examples.literal: Call your father a moment.

contrasts.says: chiamo describes what I do; chiama can ask you to act.
Like English Call the doctor, an Italian command usually leaves out the listener as subject.

mistakes.why: With singular medico, use singular il, not plural i.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

object-pronoun.explain: mi means me and ti means you when they are short objects. They go right before a verb like aspetto or aspetti: Ti aspetto, I wait for you; Mi aspetti?, will you wait for me? The verb ending still says who is waiting. non goes before the pronoun and verb. With an affirmative command to tu, the pronoun joins the end instead (aspettami); that comes later.
object-pronoun.why: In [[Ti aspetto]], ti is the person being waited for; aspetto says I am doing the waiting. English puts you after wait for.

examples.means: I'll wait for you outside.
examples.literal: You I wait for outside.

examples.means: Will you wait for me here?
examples.literal: Me you wait for here?

examples.means: I'm not waiting for you here.
examples.literal: Not you I wait for here.

contrasts.says: The subject can be left out: aspetto already says I. ti is the object, not the subject.
Italian puts ti before aspetto; English puts you after wait for.

mistakes.why: With io, use aspetto. ti still means you, the person waited for.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

di.explain: di connects a container to what is in it: una tazza di caffè, a cup of coffee. It can also connect a thing to its owner: la tazza di mia madre, my mother's cup. Here mia madre has no article; di stays separate.
di.why: English uses of for the contents and often 's for an owner. Italian uses [[di]] in both these phrases.

examples.means: I'll have a cup of coffee.
examples.literal: I take a cup of coffee.

examples.text: La tazza di mia madre è qui.
examples.means: My mother's cup is here.
examples.literal: The cup of my mother is here.

contrasts.says: la tazza di mia madre names the owner; la mia tazza uses my.
When di meets a definite article, it joins it, as in della macchina.

mistakes.wrong: La tazza di mio madre è qui.
mistakes.right: La tazza di mia madre è qui.
mistakes.why: mia agrees with madre, a feminine word.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

because.explain: perché can join an action to its reason: Resto a letto perché voglio dormire. In a direct question it asks why: Perché non dormi? A reason clause can come before or after the main clause. It follows Italian clause order, without a special rule sending the verb to the end.
because.why: The same word, [[perché]], expresses because in a reason and why in a question. The situation and sentence structure distinguish them.

examples.text: Resto a letto perché voglio dormire.
examples.means: I'm staying in bed because I want to sleep.
examples.literal: I stay in bed because I want sleep.

examples.means: Why aren't you sleeping?
examples.literal: Why not you sleep?

contrasts.says: At the start of Perché non dormi?, perché asks for the reason.
voglio takes the infinitive dormire, even inside a reason clause.

mistakes.wrong: Resto a letto perché io vuole dormire.
mistakes.right: Resto a letto perché voglio dormire.
mistakes.why: For the speaker, volere is voglio. The reason clause still needs its own correct verb form.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 41–60, open to correction.

partitive.explain: del can mean some before a masculine singular mass noun: del caffè, del latte, del cibo. It specifies no exact amount. un po' di says a little of something: un po' di acqua. po' is the shortened form of poco and keeps its apostrophe. Partitive forms agree with the following noun; their forms look like di plus a definite article. Context tells an amount from an of-the relationship. Italian can also use a bare mass noun; adding del is not always required.
partitive.why: English some can correspond to [[del]] when an unspecified amount is meant. The construction is optional in many ordinary requests.

examples.means: I'd like some coffee.
examples.literal: I would like some coffee.

examples.means: Do you want a little water?
examples.literal: You want a little of water?

contrasts.says: della in della macchina means of the car in an ownership phrase. A partitive uses the same family of forms for an amount.
Italian keeps di in un po' di acqua; English says a little water without of.

mistakes.why: caffè is masculine, so its partitive is del.

mistakes.wrong: Tu vuole un po' di acqua?
mistakes.why: With tu the form is vuoi, not vuole.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 41–60, open to correction.

negative-words.explain: With niente, nessuno or mai after the verb, standard neutral statements normally also use non: Non compro niente; Non conosco nessuno; Non bevo mai latte. This is one negative meaning, not two negatives canceling out. When niente or nessuno is before the verb as its subject, it normally supplies the negation without non: Niente è pronto; Nessuno viene. In questions and some other contexts, mai can mean ever. This lesson uses non ... mai for never.
negative-words.why: Italian often uses [[non]] together with a later negative word. English instead commonly uses not with anything or anyone, or never by itself.

examples.means: I'm not buying anything today.
examples.literal: Not I buy anything today.

examples.means: Nobody is coming tonight.
examples.literal: Nobody comes this evening.

examples.means: I never drink milk.
examples.literal: Not I drink ever milk.

contrasts.says: non still comes before the conjugated verb and any preceding short object pronouns.
Nessuno is singular in Nessuno viene, just as nobody takes comes in English.

mistakes.why: The subject nessuno takes third-person singular viene.
The speaker uses compro. The two negative words are correct.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 41–60, open to correction.

subjunctive.explain: In standard Italian, penso che and spero che normally introduce a subjunctive for an opinion or hope about a present or later situation. essere gives sia and potere gives possa with a singular subject: Penso che mia madre sia a casa; Spero che lui possa venire. These singular forms cover io, tu and lui/lei/Lei, so context or an explicit subject identifies the person. possiamo has the same spelling in the present indicative and subjunctive. che itself does not select the mood. With the same subject, an infinitive is often natural: Spero di dormire. Indicative alternatives occur in conversational Italian; they are not used as universally wrong answers here.
subjunctive.why: The verb form after [[penso che]] or [[spero che]] can mark the clause as an opinion or hope rather than a separate assertion.

examples.text: Penso che sia una buona idea.
examples.means: I think it's a good idea.
examples.literal: I think that is a good idea.

examples.means: I hope he can come.
examples.literal: I hope that he can come.

examples.text: Spero di dormire a casa stasera.
examples.means: I hope to sleep at home tonight.
examples.literal: I hope to sleep at home this evening.

contrasts.says: possiamo can be a present indicative or a present subjunctive. The surrounding construction tells its role.
spero di plus an infinitive naturally keeps the subject the same: I hope to sleep.

mistakes.wrong: Penso che mio madre sia a casa.
mistakes.right: Penso che mia madre sia a casa.
mistakes.why: mia agrees with the feminine noun madre. The form sia is correct.
lui requires singular possa, not the noi form possiamo.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 41–60, open to correction.

ci.explain: ci can stand for a place already understood in the conversation. It usually comes before a conjugated verb: Ci vado, I am going there; Ci andiamo insieme, we are going there together. In Alle tre ci sono, sono is first-person singular and ci refers to the known place: I will be there at three. In Ci sono due tazze sul tavolo, ci sono introduces the existence of two cups. With piacere, ci instead means to us. Later lessons can extend ci to complements selected by particular verbs; it cannot replace every prepositional phrase.
ci.why: Instead of repeating a place, Italian can put [[ci]] before the verb. English usually puts there after the verb.

examples.means: I'm going there tonight.
examples.literal: There I go this evening.

examples.means: I'll be there at three o'clock.
examples.literal: At the three there I am.

examples.text: Ci sono due tazze sul tavolo.
examples.means: There are two cups on the table.
examples.literal: There are two cups on the table.

contrasts.says: Existential ci sono introduces a plural noun, as in ci sono due tazze. In alle tre ci sono, I am saying I will be present.
In Ci piace questo caffè, ci means to us, not there.

mistakes.why: The noi form of andare is andiamo. ci names the place, not the subject.
With io, use sono, not the tu form sei.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 41–60, open to correction.

gli-le.explain: gli and le are short indirect-object pronouns: to him and to her. With dare they identify the person receiving something: Gli do il numero; Non le do il tuo numero. The subject of do is still I. Written Le can mean polite to you; it addresses the listener rather than naming a woman. Capitals help signal the intended use, but context is essential. These short pronouns normally precede a conjugated verb, including a modal as in Gli posso dare il numero. They can also attach in infinitive and command constructions when those are taught. For plural to them, loro is traditional and gli is widespread in contemporary Italian, especially speech; the singular examples here do not teach that distinction as an absolute right-versus-wrong rule.
gli-le.why: In [[Gli do il numero]], gli names the recipient. It does not tell who gives the number: do already says I give.

examples.means: I'll give him my number.
examples.literal: To him I give the my number.

examples.text: Non le do il tuo numero.
examples.means: I'm not giving her your number.
examples.literal: Not to her I give the your number.

examples.text: Le posso dare il numero adesso.
examples.means: I can give you the number now (polite).
examples.literal: To you I can give the number now.

contrasts.says: la in La conosco is a direct object, her. le in le do il numero is an indirect object, to her.
Le in the polite example means to you, not to her. The speaker is giving the number to the person addressed.

mistakes.why: numero is masculine and takes il mio.

mistakes.wrong: Io Le puoi dare il numero adesso.
mistakes.right: Le posso dare il numero adesso.
mistakes.why: The giver is the speaker, so the modal is posso. Le is the polite recipient.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 41–60, open to correction.

essere-perfect.explain: andare, venire, arrivare and rimanere use essere as their helper in the passato prossimo. The participle agrees with the subject: sono andato for a male speaker, sono andata for a female speaker; sei arrivato for a male listener, sei arrivata for a female listener. The ordinary participle endings are -o and -a for singular subjects, -i for a masculine or mixed plural, and -e for a feminine plural. The helper changes with the person too. Learn auxiliary choice with each verb: movement by itself does not select essere, and camminare takes avere. The inherited short rule about going, coming and staying is a useful cue for these particular verbs, not a rule covering every movement verb.
essere-perfect.why: Compare [[sono andato]] with [[ho camminato]]. The first verb selects essere and agrees with the subject; the second uses avere.

examples.means: I went home yesterday.
examples.literal: Yesterday I am gone to home.

examples.means: Did you go to the doctor?
examples.literal: You are gone to the doctor?

examples.text: Mia madre è venuta alle tre.
examples.means: My mother came at three o'clock.
examples.literal: My mother is come at the three.

examples.text: Ho camminato fino a casa e ho aspettato.
examples.means: I walked home and waited.
examples.literal: I have walked up to home and I have waited.

contrasts.says: camminare and aspettare use avere in these past events. andare and venire use essere.
With essere in these examples, the participle agrees with the person who went, came or stayed.

mistakes.wrong: Mia madre è venuto alle tre.
mistakes.right: Mia madre è venuta alle tre.
mistakes.why: The feminine subject mia madre requires venuta.

mistakes.wrong: Ieri io sei andato a casa.
mistakes.why: For the speaker, the helper is sono. Here andato is said by a male speaker.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 41–60, open to correction.

reflexive.explain: chiamarsi is the naming form of chiamare. In si chiama, si points back to the person whose name is being asked about. It is part of the naming construction, not an extra person receiving a call. With a singular third-person subject, including polite Lei, use si chiama. Here the subject is moglie: Come si chiama Sua moglie? asks for your wife's name. Other reflexive verbs may describe actions done to oneself, and some plural constructions describe reciprocal actions; learn their meanings with the verb.
reflexive.why: Italian asks how someone calls herself or himself: [[si chiama]]. Natural English asks what the person's name is.

examples.means: What's your wife's name (polite)?
examples.literal: How herself calls your wife?

examples.text: Non so come si chiama Sua moglie.
examples.means: I don't know your wife's name (polite).
examples.literal: Not I know how herself calls your wife.

contrasts.says: The pronoun si refers to the subject of chiama; an object such as ti in Ti chiamo refers to the person called.
Sua here means your, politely. It agrees with moglie; it does not say the listener is a woman.

mistakes.why: moglie is feminine, so its possessive is Sua. The naming construction si chiama is correct.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 61–80, open to correction.

adverbs.explain: Adverbs do not change to agree with a man, a woman or a plural subject. quasi describes how close something is to being true: Sono quasi pronto; Siamo quasi a casa. sicuramente adds certainty to a statement. Many adverbs are formed from an adjective's feminine singular form plus -mente, with spelling changes such as dropping a final e in some words. Learn the spelling with each word. Other adverbs have their own forms. bene describes doing something well, while buono describes something good. Position follows the intended meaning: quasi un'ora means almost an hour, and quasi pronto means almost ready.
adverbs.why: The describing word [[pronto]] can change with the speaker, but [[quasi]] stays the same.

examples.means: I'm almost ready.
examples.literal: I am almost ready.

examples.means: I waited almost an hour.
examples.literal: I have waited almost an hour.

examples.text: Ho sicuramente bisogno di un altro minuto.
examples.means: I definitely need another minute.
examples.literal: I have definitely need of an other minute.

contrasts.says: Adjectives such as pronto and pronta agree. Adverbs such as quasi and sicuramente do not.
quasi can come directly before the expression it qualifies, like almost in almost an hour.

mistakes.why: The speaker uses sono. quasi remains unchanged.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 61–80, open to correction.

comparative.explain: prima can compare a time with another time: arrivi prima means you arrive earlier than expected or than a time already mentioned. To name a person as the comparison, use prima di: Arrivo prima di te. un minuto prima says how much earlier. prima also means first when ordering actions, as in Prima ho chiamato mia madre. The situation distinguishes first from earlier. Other types of comparison have their own forms and links; this lesson introduces comparisons of time.
comparative.why: English adds -er to early. Italian uses [[prima]] for earlier and [[prima di]] for earlier than.

examples.means: Today I'm arriving earlier than you.
examples.literal: Today I arrive earlier than you.

examples.means: Can you come a minute earlier?
examples.literal: You can come a minute earlier?

contrasts.says: prima qualifies when someone arrives, without changing for gender or number.
After di, use the stressed pronoun te for familiar you, as in prima di te.

mistakes.wrong: Oggi io arrivi prima di te.
mistakes.why: The subject io requires arrivo. prima di te expresses the comparison.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 61–80, open to correction.

ne.explain: With a quantity, ne stands for a noun already known from the conversation: Ne ho due means I have two of them. It can refer to a substance too: Ne abbiamo abbastanza, we have enough of it. The quantity remains after the verb, including uno for a masculine noun or una for a feminine noun. In Non ne ho, the negative says I have none. ne normally comes before the conjugated verb here; non comes before ne. It is not the subject and does not determine the verb ending. Quanti ne vuoi? keeps the question word before ne and the verb. The question word agrees with what is counted: quanti for books, quante for photos. These lessons use simple tenses; past-participle agreement and other meanings of ne come later.
ne.why: English can leave of them unsaid in I have two. Italian uses [[ne]] to refer back to the things counted.

examples.means: I have two.
examples.literal: Of them I have two.

examples.means: We have enough.
examples.literal: Of it we have enough.

examples.means: I don't have any.
examples.literal: Not of them I have.

contrasts.says: dei libri names an unspecified number of books; ne can refer back to books without repeating the noun.
ne precedes the conjugated verb in these sentences, as other short object pronouns do.

mistakes.why: The speaker uses ho. ne refers to the things counted, not the person who has them.
With noi, use abbiamo.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 61–80, open to correction.

imperfect.explain: The imperfetto describes a past habit, an ongoing background activity or a state. In A volte prendevamo un caffè insieme, a volte makes the repeated habit clear, and prendevamo is the noi form of the imperfect. Non prendevamo mai il caffè a casa describes a habit that never happened. By contrast, abbiamo bevuto presents a completed event. English sometimes uses the same simple past for both perspectives, or makes the habit explicit with used to. The time word alone does not select the tense: what matters is whether the speaker presents a habit or background, or a bounded event.
imperfect.why: [[prendevamo]] locates the habit in the past. It does not describe what we regularly do now.

examples.text: A volte prendevamo un caffè insieme.
examples.means: We sometimes had coffee together.
examples.literal: At times we used to have a coffee together.

examples.text: Non prendevamo mai il caffè a casa.
examples.means: We never used to have coffee at home.
examples.literal: Not we used to have ever the coffee at home.

examples.means: We had a coffee there.
examples.literal: We have drunk a coffee there.

contrasts.says: The compound past presents a completed event. The imperfect presents a past habit or background.
We had coffee can describe either a habit or one event. Italian makes the perspective visible in the verb.

mistakes.wrong: A volte noi prendeva un caffè insieme.
mistakes.right: A volte prendevamo un caffè insieme.
mistakes.why: With noi, the imperfect form is prendevamo. The explicit noi in the wrong version rules out another subject.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 81–100, open to correction.

real-condition.explain: se means if when it introduces a condition. For a real possibility, use the indicative in these examples: Se hai tempo. The other clause can describe what follows or ask someone to act: mandami la foto. A present-tense result with a clear future situation can be translated with will in English: Se hai un attimo, ti mando la foto. You can also put the condition last: Mandami il tuo numero se puoi. Neither position requires a special change in the main clause's word order. Later lessons distinguish imagined or contrary-to-fact conditions, which use different tense and mood combinations. In a question inside a sentence, se can instead mean whether.
real-condition.why: [[se]] links a possible condition to its result. [[hai]] stays an ordinary present indicative form here.

examples.text: Se hai tempo, mandami la foto.
examples.means: If you have time, send me the photo.
examples.literal: If you have time, send me the photo.

examples.text: Se hai un attimo, ti mando la foto.
examples.means: If you have a moment, I'll send you the photo.
examples.literal: If you have a moment, to you I send the photo.

examples.text: Mandami il tuo numero se puoi.
examples.means: Send me your number if you can.
examples.literal: Send me the your number if you can.

contrasts.says: The condition states a possibility, and mandami gives a request that applies in that situation.
Italian can use the present for a planned result where English uses will.

mistakes.wrong: Se tu ha tempo, mandami la foto.
mistakes.right: Se hai tempo, mandami la foto.
mistakes.why: The explicitly stated tu requires hai, not ha.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 81–100, open to correction.

modal-perfect.explain: To put a modal in the compound past, use an auxiliary and the modal's past participle, followed by the other verb's infinitive. Ho dovuto tirare forte means I had to pull hard. Ho potuto aprire la porta reports that opening the door was possible and, in this situation, was accomplished. The modal carries the past marking; aprire and tirare remain infinitives. These constructions use avere with transitive aprire and tirare. With other infinitives, auxiliary choice is more complex: the auxiliary of the infinitive can be retained, avere is also possible in many modal constructions, and the position of reflexive pronouns can affect the choice. Learn the complete construction and do not treat every avere/essere alternative as an error. These examples do not introduce the different use of an imperfect modal for past ability, intention or obligation.
modal-perfect.why: [[ho dovuto]] says had to, while [[tirare]] names the action. The modal becomes a participle rather than a second infinitive.

examples.means: I had to pull hard.
examples.literal: I have had to pull hard.

examples.text: Finalmente ho potuto aprire la porta.
examples.means: I was finally able to open the door.
examples.literal: Finally I have been able to open the door.

examples.means: We had to pull together.
examples.literal: We have had to pull together.

contrasts.says: A present modal is conjugated directly. In these compound past forms, the auxiliary is conjugated and the modal becomes a participle.
The compound tense still uses an auxiliary plus a participle. Here that participle belongs to the modal.

mistakes.why: With io, the auxiliary must be ho.

mistakes.wrong: Finalmente ho potuto aprire il porta.
mistakes.right: Finalmente ho potuto aprire la porta.
mistakes.why: porta is feminine and takes la. The modal construction ho potuto aprire is correct.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 81–100, open to correction.

combined-pronouns.explain: When two short pronouns occur together, their forms and order matter. ti becomes te before lo: te lo means it to you, with familiar singular you. The other changing forms are mi to me, ci to ce, vi to ve and si to se before lo, la, li, le or ne. The indirect gli or le combines into one written word with the next pronoun: glielo can mean it to him or it to her. The context identifies the recipient. The pair goes before the conjugated verb in these examples. With a modal, both pronouns can also attach together to the infinitive. With an affirmative tu or voi command they attach to the command. A preceding lo, la, li or le also determines the agreement of a past participle where required: detto is masculine singular after lo in Te lo ha detto mio fratello. These lessons practice te lo and glielo with masculine singular objects or a whole piece of information.
combined-pronouns.why: [[te lo]] is two written words, while [[glielo]] is one. In both, the recipient comes before the direct object.

examples.text: Il numero? Te lo mando subito.
examples.means: The number? I'll send it to you right away.
examples.literal: The number? To you it I send right away.

examples.text: Il mio numero? Glielo puoi dare.
examples.means: My number? You can give it to him.
examples.literal: The my number? To him it you can give.

examples.text: Il libro è per mia sorella, glielo porto dopo.
examples.means: The book is for my sister; I'll take it to her later.
examples.literal: The book is for my sister, to her it I take later.

examples.text: Te lo ha detto mio fratello?
examples.means: Did my brother tell you?
examples.literal: To you it has said my brother?

contrasts.says: gli or le alone identifies an indirect object. glielo combines that recipient with a masculine singular direct object.
The ordinary object-pronoun positions still apply, but the two pronouns form an ordered pair.

mistakes.wrong: Il mia numero? Glielo puoi dare.
mistakes.right: Il mio numero? Glielo puoi dare.
mistakes.why: numero is masculine, so mio agrees with it.

mistakes.wrong: Io te lo può mandare stasera.
mistakes.why: The speaker requires posso. te lo stays together before the modal.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 81–100, open to correction.

subjunctive-imperfect.explain: come se means as if and introduces an imagined comparison. For a situation simultaneous with the main clause, use the imperfect subjunctive: Parla come se abitasse in questa casa. abitasse is the third-person singular imperfect subjunctive of abitare, and fossero is the third-person plural imperfect subjunctive of essere. These forms do not by themselves mean that the situation is over: she can be speaking now as if she lived here now. The construction compares appearances or behavior with an imagined situation, without asserting that it is true. The imperfect subjunctive is also used for simultaneous or later situations after past wishes and opinions. An imagined situation earlier than the main reference point calls for a different compound form, covered later.
subjunctive-imperfect.why: [[come se]] sets up the comparison, and [[abitasse]] marks the imagined situation. English likewise uses a past-looking form in as if she lived here.

examples.text: Sembra come se mia sorella abitasse qui.
examples.means: It looks as if my sister lived here.
examples.literal: It seems as if my sister lived here.

examples.text: Parla come se abitasse in questa casa.
examples.means: She talks as if she lived in this house.
examples.literal: She talks as if she lived in this house.

examples.text: Parlano come se fossero a casa loro.
examples.means: They talk as if they were at home.
examples.literal: They talk as if they were at home their.

contrasts.says: The present subjunctive and imperfect subjunctive have different forms and uses. come se selects the imperfect subjunctive for the simultaneous comparison practiced here.
A real condition with se uses the indicative in the earlier examples. come se introduces an imagined comparison instead.

mistakes.wrong: Parla come se abitasse in questo casa.
mistakes.right: Parla come se abitasse in questa casa.
mistakes.why: casa is feminine, so this is questa. The imagined comparison uses abitasse.

mistakes.wrong: Parlano come se loro fosse a casa loro.
mistakes.right: Parlano come se fossero a casa loro.
mistakes.why: The explicit plural subject loro requires fossero, not fosse.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 81–100, open to correction.

future.explain: The futuro semplice puts the future meaning into the verb itself. For regular verbs, the endings are -ò, -ai, -à, -emo, -ete, -anno. Regular -are verbs change the a of the infinitive ending to e and drop the final e before these endings: lavorare gives lavorerò. Regular -ere and -ire verbs drop their final e. Spelling adjustments may also be needed, so learn them with each verb. Some verbs have irregular stems, including sar- for essere and avr- for avere. Accents distinguish forms such as sarò and sarà. A time such as domani can also make a present-tense sentence describe a plan: Domani sono a casa. The future is therefore not required every time English uses will. In other contexts, the future can express a guess about a present situation; the surrounding conversation supplies that reading.
future.why: Italian [[lavorerò]] is one conjugated verb. English uses will plus work.

examples.means: I'll work at home tomorrow.
examples.literal: Tomorrow I will work at home.

examples.means: I'll be at the office tomorrow.
examples.literal: Tomorrow I will be in office.

examples.means: I'll have time for you tomorrow.
examples.literal: I will have time for you tomorrow.

examples.means: I'll be home tomorrow.
examples.literal: Tomorrow I am at home.

contrasts.says: With a future time, a present form can express a plan too.
The future meaning and the person are both carried by the Italian verb form.

mistakes.why: The speaker uses sarò. The explicit io cannot take the third-person form sarà.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 101–120, open to correction.

duration.explain: When something began earlier and is still true, Italian normally uses a present tense with da. A duration answers how long: Abito qui da due anni. A starting point answers since when: da ieri means since yesterday. English normally uses a perfect tense, often a progressive one: Aspetto da un'ora means I have been waiting for an hour. Da quanto tempo asks how long a continuing situation has lasted. In a negative sentence, the same construction can say how long something has not happened: Non bevo caffè da un mese. A completed period instead uses a past tense, with per when the length is stated explicitly. fa follows a length of time and means ago; it locates an event before now rather than describing its continuing duration.
duration.why: [[da]] combines with the present when the situation continues now. English usually changes the verb to a perfect tense.

examples.means: I've lived here for two years.
examples.literal: I live here for two years.

examples.means: I've been waiting for an hour.
examples.literal: I wait for an hour.

examples.text: Non bevo caffè da un mese.
examples.means: I haven't had coffee for a month.
examples.literal: Not I drink coffee for a month.

examples.means: I waited for an hour.
examples.literal: I have waited for an hour.

examples.means: I called a year ago.
examples.literal: I have called a year ago.

contrasts.says: A completed wait uses ho aspettato. A wait still in progress can use aspetto da.
Italian present + da often corresponds to English have been doing or have done.

mistakes.why: The number due requires the plural anni.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 101–120, open to correction.

relative.explain: A relative clause identifies or describes a noun. che can stand for its subject: La persona che lavora qui è gentile. It can also stand for its direct object: Il lavoro che faccio è difficile. In that second sentence, the speaker does the work, and che stands for the work. English can omit an object relative: the job I want. Italian keeps che: il lavoro che voglio. che does not change for the gender or number of the noun. For a place, dove means where: la città dove abito. A relative clause has its own subject and verb; the main verb still agrees with the main clause subject. A relative is different from che introducing a statement after a verb of saying or thinking: the relative points back to a noun. Later lessons introduce cui with a preposition for other grammatical roles.
relative.why: [[che]] keeps the noun connected to the description even when English leaves that connection unspoken.

examples.text: Questo è il lavoro che voglio.
examples.means: This is the job I want.
examples.literal: This is the job that I want.

examples.text: Il lavoro che faccio è difficile.
examples.means: The work I do is difficult.
examples.literal: The work that I do is difficult.

examples.text: La persona che lavora qui è gentile.
examples.means: The person who works here is kind.
examples.literal: The person who works here is kind.

examples.text: Cerco lavoro nella città dove abito.
examples.means: I'm looking for work in the city where I live.
examples.literal: I look for work in the city where I live.

contrasts.says: dove asks where in a question. After a place noun here, it introduces a relative description.
An English object relative can be omitted. Italian che remains.

mistakes.wrong: Questo è il lavoro che io vuole.
mistakes.right: Questo è il lavoro che voglio.
mistakes.why: The explicit io requires voglio. che stands for the job wanted and is not the subject of vuole.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 101–120, open to correction.

gerund.explain: The gerundio is a form such as studiando or cucinando. Regular -are verbs use -ando; regular -ere and -ire verbs use -endo. Learn irregular forms with their verbs. With stare it describes an action in progress: sta leggendo. On its own it can give the means or an accompanying action: Studiando ho capito questa regola means I understood this rule by studying. Mia madre ascolta la musica cucinando means my mother listens to music while cooking. In these examples, the same person does both actions. A gerund with no subject of its own is understood as the main verb's subject, so here it can't describe someone else's action. The gerund does not change for person, gender or number. For posture, use essere or stare with seduto or seduta. Sono seduto qui da un'ora describes a posture continuing now: I have been sitting here for an hour.
gerund.why: [[studiando]] gives the means of understanding; [[cucinando]] gives an accompanying action. The main verb supplies the person and time.

examples.means: I understood this rule by studying.
examples.literal: Studying I have understood this rule.

examples.text: Mia madre ascolta la musica cucinando.
examples.means: My mother listens to music while cooking.
examples.literal: My mother listens to the music cooking.

examples.means: I talk on the phone while walking.
examples.literal: I talk on the phone walking.

examples.text: Mio padre è seduto sul divano e legge.
examples.means: My father is sitting on the sofa and reading.
examples.literal: My father is seated on the sofa and reads.

contrasts.says: stare plus a gerund marks an action in progress. The gerund alone can link an accompanying action to the main one.
A gerund is invariable. The posture word seduto changes to seduta for a woman.

mistakes.why: The compound past needs the participle capito after ho. studiando explains how the understanding happened.

mistakes.wrong: Mio padre è seduta sul divano e legge.
mistakes.right: Mio padre è seduto sul divano e legge.
mistakes.why: The posture word agrees with padre, a masculine singular noun.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 121–140, open to correction.

past-perfect.explain: The trapassato prossimo places an event before another past reference point. Use imperfect avere or essere plus a past participle. Avevo già mangiato quando hai chiamato says the eating was already complete when the call happened. The reference point can be stated or understood from the conversation. Auxiliary choice follows the other compound tenses: mangiare takes avere; uscire takes essere here. With essere, the participle agrees with the subject: mio fratello era uscito, mia sorella era uscita. With avere, ordinary compound-tense agreement rules still apply; these participles do not agree with the subject. The auxiliary supplies person and number: avevo, avevi, aveva, avevamo, avevano. English uses had plus a past participle but does not change had for the person. An imperfect alone gives background; this compound tense places an event earlier.
past-perfect.why: [[avevo]] plus [[mangiato]] says had eaten. [[era]] plus [[uscita]] says had gone out, with a feminine singular participle.

examples.text: Avevo già mangiato quando hai chiamato.
examples.means: I had already eaten when you called.
examples.literal: I had already eaten when you have called.

examples.text: Quando sono arrivato, mio fratello era già uscito.
examples.means: When I arrived, my brother had already gone out.
examples.literal: When I am arrived, my brother was already gone out.

examples.text: Mia sorella era già uscita quando ho chiamato.
examples.means: My sister had already gone out when I called.
examples.literal: My sister was already gone out when I have called.

examples.text: Non avevamo mai visto quel film.
examples.means: We had never seen that movie.
examples.literal: Not we had ever seen that movie.

contrasts.says: ho mangiato presents a completed past event. avevo mangiato places that event before another past reference point.
The auxiliary is imperfect, but the whole construction is a compound tense expressing an earlier past event.
The same auxiliary choice and agreement apply: è uscita becomes era uscita.

mistakes.wrong: Avevo già mangiare quando hai chiamato.
mistakes.right: Avevo già mangiato quando hai chiamato.
mistakes.why: The auxiliary avevo needs the past participle mangiato here, not the infinitive mangiare.

mistakes.wrong: Mia sorella era già uscito quando ho chiamato.
mistakes.right: Mia sorella era già uscita quando ho chiamato.
mistakes.why: With essere, the participle agrees with the feminine singular subject sorella.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 121–140, open to correction.

passive.explain: A passive makes the receiver of an action the subject. The verb essere supplies the tense and person, and the past participle agrees with that subject. In La casa è stata venduta, both stata and venduta are feminine singular to agree with casa. The complete construction means the house has been sold. Da introduces the agent, the person doing the action. In a simple tense, venire can replace essere to emphasize an action: Il caffè viene preparato da mio padre. Viene here is part of the passive, not a statement that the coffee comes somewhere. With a plural subject, use a plural auxiliary and participle: Questi libri vengono letti a scuola. Use essere, not venire, to form a compound passive such as è stata venduta. Essere plus a participle can also describe a state; an expression such as ogni giorno makes a repeated action clear in Il cibo è preparato qui ogni giorno.
passive.why: The receiver becomes the subject: [[la casa]] agrees with [[stata venduta]]. [[da]] introduces the agent when one is named.

examples.means: The house has been sold.
examples.literal: The house is been sold.

examples.text: Il caffè viene preparato da mio padre.
examples.means: The coffee is made by my father.
examples.literal: The coffee is prepared by my father.

examples.text: Questi libri vengono letti a scuola.
examples.means: These books are read at school.
examples.literal: These books are read at school.

contrasts.says: An active compound past identifies what someone did. A passive makes the receiver of the action its subject.
The passive participle agrees with the subject, including in a compound passive.

mistakes.why: Venduta must agree with the feminine singular casa.

mistakes.wrong: Questi libri viene letti a scuola.
mistakes.right: Questi libri vengono letti a scuola.
mistakes.why: The plural subject libri needs the plural auxiliary vengono.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 141–160, open to correction.

si-impersonal.explain: Si can describe people in general without naming a subject. Qui si mangia bene means people eat well here, or the food is good here. The impersonal construction normally uses a singular verb. It does not mean someone eats themselves. With a transitive verb and an expressed patient, si can instead form a passive: In questo quartiere si vendono case. Case is plural, so vendono is plural. The sentence means houses are sold in this neighborhood. This differs from reflexive or reciprocal si, where the action refers back to the subject. With a reflexive verb in an impersonal construction, the pronouns are ci si rather than si si. Learn those complete expressions as they arrive. The present examples use mangiare impersonally without an object and vendere passively with case.
si-impersonal.why: In [[si mangia]], si refers to people in general. In [[si vendono case]], the plural thing being sold controls the verb.

examples.means: People eat well here.
examples.literal: Here people eat well.

examples.means: People eat here at two.
examples.literal: Here people eat at the two.

examples.text: In questo quartiere si vendono case.
examples.means: Houses are sold in this neighborhood.
examples.literal: In this neighborhood [passive] sell houses.

contrasts.says: Reflexive si refers back to a particular subject. Impersonal si leaves the people unspecified.
Passive si and essere plus a participle both allow a patient to be the subject, but their forms differ.

mistakes.why: Impersonal si takes a third-person singular verb: si mangia. The -iamo ending belongs to noi.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 141–160, open to correction.

superlative.explain: The relative superlative selects the highest or lowest degree within a group. Use a definite article with più or meno and an adjective: la casa più grande, the biggest house. The comparison group can be stated with di, contracted with an article when required: la casa più grande del quartiere. The article belongs to the whole noun phrase; it does not need repeating immediately before più. Migliore means better, and la scelta migliore means the best choice. Do not add più to migliore. An absolute superlative describes a high degree without choosing a member of a group. A common ending is -issimo, with gender and number agreement: grandissima is feminine singular and means very big. Not every adjective forms its superlative in exactly the same way; learn unfamiliar forms with the adjective.
superlative.why: The article and [[più grande]] identify the biggest within a group. [[grandissima]] simply expresses a high degree.

examples.text: Questa è la casa più grande del quartiere.
examples.means: This is the biggest house in the neighborhood.
examples.literal: This is the house most big of the neighborhood.

examples.text: Questa casa è grandissima, ma costa troppo.
examples.means: This house is very big, but it costs too much.
examples.literal: This house is very big, but costs too much.

examples.text: Questa è la scelta migliore per noi.
examples.means: This is the best choice for us.
examples.literal: This is the choice best for us.

contrasts.says: Più grande della nostra compares two houses. La casa più grande del quartiere selects the biggest in the neighborhood.
The ending in grandissima agrees with the feminine singular noun casa.

mistakes.wrong: Questa è la scelta più migliore per noi.
mistakes.right: Questa è la scelta migliore per noi.
mistakes.why: Migliore already expresses the comparative degree; with the definite article it gives the best choice.

mistakes.wrong: Questa casa è grandissimi, ma costa troppo.
mistakes.right: Questa casa è grandissima, ma costa troppo.
mistakes.why: Casa is feminine singular, so the ending is -issima.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 141–160, open to correction.

subjunctive-perfect.explain: The subjunctive perfect combines a present subjunctive auxiliary, such as abbia or sia, with a past participle. In these examples, the event comes before the present opinion, hope, or feeling. In Credo che mio padre abbia già mangiato, the eating comes before the belief being expressed. Spero che tu abbia letto la notizia hopes that the reading has already happened. Choose avere or essere as in the verb's other compound forms. With essere, agree the participle with the subject: sia venuto for a man, sia venuta for a woman. Abbia and sia have the same form for io, tu, lui, lei, and polite Lei, so include the subject when it is needed to identify the person. The subjunctive does not always mean uncertainty: Sono contento che tu sia venuto can express happiness about a real visit. Contento describes the speaker, whereas venuto describes the visitor.
subjunctive-perfect.why: The auxiliary marks the subjunctive, while the participle places the event earlier: [[abbia letto]], [[sia venuto]].

examples.text: Credo che mio padre abbia già mangiato.
examples.means: I think my father has already eaten.
examples.literal: I believe that my father has already eaten.

examples.text: Spero che tu abbia letto la notizia.
examples.means: I hope you've read the news.
examples.literal: I hope that you have read the piece of news.

examples.text: Sono contento che tu sia venuto.
examples.means: I'm glad you came.
examples.literal: I am happy that you are come.

contrasts.says: The simple present subjunctive can refer to a current or later event. The subjunctive perfect presents an earlier event.
The choice of essere and the participle agreement also apply here, but the auxiliary is subjunctive.

mistakes.wrong: Spero che tu abbia leggo la notizia.
mistakes.right: Spero che tu abbia letto la notizia.
mistakes.why: A compound form needs the participle letto, not the finite present leggo.

mistakes.wrong: Sono contento che tu sia venire.
mistakes.right: Sono contento che tu sia venuto.
mistakes.why: Use the participle venuto with sia, agreeing with a male visitor. Venire is an infinitive.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 161–180, open to correction.

unreal-condition.explain: When imagining a different situation now or later, Italian commonly uses se followed by an imperfect subjunctive, with a present conditional for the result. Se avessi tempo, verrei da te means If I had time, I would come to your place. Avessi imagines having time, and verrei gives the result. Se fossi in te, lo farei is the usual way to say If I were you, I would do it. The conditional also has a compound past form: a conditional auxiliary, such as avrei or sarei, plus a participle. Avrei voluto restare means I would have liked to stay. Sarei venuto means I would have come, with venuto agreeing with a male speaker; a female speaker says sarei venuta. In these lessons the following explanation tells why the intended action did not happen. The past conditional can also report a future event from a past viewpoint.
unreal-condition.why: Separate the imagined condition from its result: [[se avessi]] gives the condition, and [[verrei]] gives what would follow.

examples.text: Se avessi tempo, verrei da te.
examples.means: If I had time, I would come to your place.
examples.literal: If I had time, I would come to you.

examples.text: Se fossi in te, lo farei.
examples.means: If I were you, I'd do it.
examples.literal: If I were in you, it I would do.

examples.text: Avrei voluto restare, ma dovevo lavorare.
examples.means: I would have liked to stay, but I had to work.
examples.literal: I would have wanted stay, but I had to work.

examples.means: I would have come, but I had to work.
examples.literal: I would be come, but I had to work.

contrasts.says: A real condition uses indicative forms. This pattern imagines a different present or future situation.
The conditional gives the result. Its compound past uses an auxiliary plus a participle.

mistakes.wrong: Se avessi tempo, io verrebbe da te.
mistakes.right: Se avessi tempo, verrei da te.
mistakes.why: The first-person conditional is verrei. Verrebbe cannot agree with explicit io.
The past conditional needs the participle venuto, not the infinitive venire.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 161–180, open to correction.

causative.explain: Fare followed directly by an infinitive can describe arranging for someone else to do an action. Faccio riparare la macchina means I am having the car repaired. Faccio identifies the person arranging it, and riparare names the work. The mechanic or other person doing it need not be named. In Mi faccio controllare la vista, mi identifies the person receiving the check: I am having my eyes checked. The article la is natural with the body or bodily faculty; English uses my. Fare can also mean making someone do something, so context determines whether an action is arranged or imposed. Keep the second verb infinitive and add no linking a or di in this construction.
causative.why: The person expressed by [[faccio]] arranges the action expressed by [[riparare]] or [[controllare]].

examples.means: I'm having my eyes checked.
examples.literal: For myself I have check the eyesight.

examples.means: I'm having my leg checked.
examples.literal: For myself I have check the leg.

examples.text: Faccio riparare la macchina dopo l'incidente.
examples.means: I'm having the car repaired after the accident.
examples.literal: I have repair the car after the accident.

contrasts.says: The passive makes the receiver the subject. A causative can instead make the person arranging the action the subject.
Different verbs take different links. Causative fare takes a bare infinitive.

mistakes.wrong: Faccio riparo la macchina dopo l'incidente.
mistakes.right: Faccio riparare la macchina dopo l'incidente.
mistakes.why: After causative faccio, use the infinitive riparare, not riparo.

mistakes.wrong: Mi faccio di controllare la vista.
mistakes.why: Causative fare takes the infinitive directly, without di.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 161–180, open to correction.

diminutive.explain: Italian has established noun forms that express small size, affection, or a modest way of presenting something. Here regalo becomes regalino, tazza becomes tazzina, libro becomes libretto, and casa becomes casetta. The endings are -ino, -ina, -etto, and -etta. These examples keep their base noun's gender: un regalino and un libretto are masculine; una tazzina and una casetta are feminine. Un attimino is a familiar way of asking for just a moment. It does not promise an exact length of time. A little gift can be called un regalino to sound affectionate or modest even when its physical size is not the point. Learn the established form and its meaning rather than adding any ending to any noun. Some diminutives also have separate dictionary meanings. Panchina is the ordinary word for a bench in this lesson; its spelling alone does not make it an example of these four endings.
diminutive.why: The ending can add smallness or affection to a familiar noun: [[casa → casetta]], [[regalo → regalino]]. Agreement still follows the resulting noun.

examples.text: Ho portato un regalino per tua madre.
examples.means: I brought a little gift for your mother.
examples.literal: I have brought a little gift for your mother.

examples.text: La tua tazzina è ancora sulla panchina.
examples.means: Your little cup is still on the bench.
examples.literal: The your little cup is still on the bench.

examples.means: I've already read this little book.
examples.literal: I have already read this little book.

examples.text: La panchina è davanti alla casetta.
examples.means: The bench is in front of the little house.
examples.literal: The bench is in front of the little house.

examples.text: Aspetta un attimino, il caffè è quasi pronto.
examples.means: Wait just a moment; the coffee is almost ready.
examples.literal: Wait a little moment, the coffee is almost ready.

contrasts.says: Diminutives still need articles and adjectives that agree with the noun.
English may use little or small, or express the friendly tone without a separate adjective.

mistakes.wrong: Ho portato una regalino per tua madre.
mistakes.right: Ho portato un regalino per tua madre.
mistakes.why: Regalino is masculine, so use un rather than una.

mistakes.wrong: La tuo tazzina è ancora sulla panchina.
mistakes.right: La tua tazzina è ancora sulla panchina.
mistakes.why: Tazzina is feminine. The possessive is tua, as with tazza.
